title: Lojong Teaching 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces the Lojong mind-training slogans, starting with a story of Atisha, who leaves his wedding night at age eleven after a vision of Tara and later brings an ill-tempered Bengali servant boy to Tibet to give him something to practice with. Nomon then walks through the first three of the seven points: "Regard all dharmas as dreams," with an account of holding a hard work situation more lightly, and "Drive all blames into one," with a long reading from Chögyam Trungpa on taking the blame. A participant questions that slogan, and Nomon asks the group to try it and report back. "Be grateful to everyone" follows, and Nomon closes by singing a Kenyan lullaby once sung to a young son.

sentences.text: These teachings are known as lo-jong, which is a Tibetan word.
You didn't know you were coming to Tibetan tonight, but you are.
Lo-jong means mind training, literally: lo means mind, jong means training.
They come to us as a set of slogans which are attributed to an Indian Buddhist teacher named Atisha, or possibly his teacher, who really knows.
I want to tell you a story about Atisha.
It's fun to learn about one's ancestors.
Atisha lived in what is now Bangladesh from about 980 to 1050 common era, and he's an important teacher for all the Tibetan lineages.
He's Indian, ostensibly, there's no India then, but he's an important ancestor for all the Tibetan lineages.
Along with Marpa, who you may have heard of, who's also a famous teacher, and someone else named Khön Könchok Gyalpo, who I've never heard of.
The three of them together are credited with founding the first important Tibetan Buddhist lineage, which went on to become all the other currently extant Tibetan lineages.
But Buddhism already existed in Tibet, so it's a revival, I guess.
All school and lineage histories are a little bit suspect historically, but they're enthusiastic and devotional and great.
Pretty much everyone in the Kagyu and the Sakya and the Kadam schools sees Atisha as a lineage ancestor.
Everyone except the Nyingma guys, who feel like they had an earlier transmission.
Similar to Shakyamuni Buddha, Atisha was a prince of a small kingdom or principality.
I was thinking, what's a funny coincidence?
Why are they all princes?
Then I realized, well, it's exactly the same as today, isn't it?
The working stiffs don't have time.
You have to be upper middle class to have time to practice enough that you could come up with all this stuff.
I hope that we're learning and sharing that anybody can practice, but probably you have to be a full-timer to do the kind of stuff that someone like Atisha did.
Although, when Atisha was born, there were all kinds of miracles, just like there were when baby Buddha was born.
In the Buddha's case, it wasn't until he was in his early twenties that he realized, something's a little funny here.
I'm not totally content with my life in the palace.
But Atisha figured this out a lot earlier.
When he was a toddler, he figured this out.
Apparently they took him to some kind of public gathering when he was 18 months old, and he started teaching Dharma.
So he figured it out a little earlier.
By the time he was 10, he had mastered all of the significant teachings of Buddhism around, in the local area.
He sort of exhausted the local resources.
So when he was 11, his parents decided they'd really better marry him off and try to settle him down.
You can guess what happened next.
Oh, you guessed it.
On his wedding night, 11 years old, his wedding night, the young Atisha had a vision.
Tara appeared.
Tara is one of the manifestations of Avalokiteshvara, the Indo-Tibetan manifestation.
And this lady here, this is the Chinese manifestation over here, the Bodhisattva of Compassion.
Tara has different forms and different colors and so on.
I don't know that much about Tara.
But anyway, Tara was an important figure for Atisha throughout his life.
She often came to him in visions and helped him figure out what to do.
She appeared and told him that being a rich married royal person was going to be a distraction.
She said, apparently, as an elephant sinks deeply into the swamp, a hero would sink into the mire of lust.
If you lived that way, you would be like an elephant sunk in a swamp, sunk in the mire of lust.
Accordingly, he slipped out, as they do, found a local wise man.
There's always a local wise man.
Then he ran off to one of the great Buddhist universities of the day, the great Buddhist university of Nalanda, to become a monk.
So maybe then he's 12 or 13.
Nalanda, by the way, is where Shantideva taught about 100 years prior to that, if you've heard of Shantideva.
It seems very likely that all these Buddhist hagiographies were written by men, because there's no mention in the summary of Atisha's biography about what happened to his fiancée.
She's not even a character in the story.
Or how his mother felt.
But I did recently read a sixth century account from Thailand, a sixth century Thai account, about what happened when Shakyamuni Buddha returned to his family for the first time in Kapilavastu.
It's a sort of essay posing as a sutra, and it's called Bimba's Lament.
Bimba is another name for Shakyamuni Buddha Siddhartha's wife.
It's all about how miserable and upset and angry she is.
Maybe these issues weren't totally ignored, and another time we'll study that.
It's really interesting.
But all that aside, it's a difficult aspect of these canonical stories of these great teachers.
It does seem clear that some kind of renunciation is essential.
It doesn't seem like it's really going to work to just go about our business, do all the things we usually do, and then add dharma on top of that, like another hobby.
It seems like we have to in some way let go of something, or in some way transform or recreate, re-imagine our life to really feel the potential of dharma practice.
We have to let go of something.
But does that mean that we should renounce our families?
I always make the joke that the court system would be tracking down Siddhartha for abandonment and making him pay child support.
Or were these young men just confused and heavily influenced by the socio-cultural environment, and they thought that the only way forward was to abandon their families?
Or is there something inherent about deep practice that means we have to abandon everything and live alone?
One thing I realized is that the technology of the times is probably one factor that's worth noticing.
If I were to convince my family that I should go off to Nalanda University and study Buddhism, we would still be in contact.
We'd be on the phone.
We'd be on Skype.
We'd be emailing.
We'd be writing letters.
I'd probably be talking to them every day.
We can stay connected at a distance and stay in relationship in a way that wasn't available even to the princes of tenth century India.
It probably took a month or two to travel to Nalanda from Bangladesh, so if you left, you left.
I don't want to excuse their behavior, but maybe that was part of it.
If you wanted to study and there weren't too many places that you could seriously study, you left.
That's how it was understood.
Once you left, you were gone.
But the next part of Atisha's story actually feels a little better to us than Shakyamuni's story.
Shakyamuni was in the neighborhood, but he was studying all these ascetic practices and working with all these teachers for seven years.
He could have gone home for a visit, you know what I mean?
Nobody's stopping him.
But he didn't.
Not until after his enlightenment, once he was teaching, did he go.
The story of Bhima's lament, which is definitely an exaggeration, said that when he returned to Kapilavastu, this is Shakyamuni now, he showed up with 64,000 monks.
The ground was a little bit uneven, and they were having a little trouble getting around because there were 64,000 monks.
There were probably 10,000 people in the town, so 64,000 monks show up.
Miraculously, everything got smooth and easy to walk, and maybe there was miraculously more room for them.
It was this huge thing that he showed up with.
He didn't quietly head home for a little visit.
But anyway, in the case of Atisha, the ancestor of these Lojong teachings, he did sneak off to practice for maybe a year or maybe a couple of years at Nalanda University.
The story is that he completed all the main training on the meditations on emptiness, and he was advised to go off to an independent teacher, a Black Mountain Yogi.
I love the sound of that.
It's time for you to go study with the Black Mountain Yogi.
The Black Mountain Yogi checked out his understanding with various magical tests and gave him some teachings, I think it said for 18 days.
He was willing to teach him for 18 days.

Then the Black Mountain Yogi told Atisha that before he would train him further, Atisha had to go home and receive his parents' permission to be a monk, that he wouldn't really be able to study deeply if he had that unresolved karma of having left home.
I thought that was interesting.
Apparently it did work out.
Atisha persistently made the argument that the best way he could repay his parents' kindness to him was to renounce luxury and learn how people can really settle their hearts.
So he did that, and his dad was okay, but his mom was reluctant, and they said okay.
Later he traveled on another huge journey, an even bigger journey, to Sumatra.
Indonesia was a big place for Buddhism in the tenth century, and there was an important teacher in Sumatra.
He went there for 12 years, and he went to another North Indian monastic university called Vikramasila.
Then he was invited to Tibet by an emissary of one of the Tibetan kings.
I guess Tibet was a few kingdoms.
The Western Kingdom sent an emissary that had heard of Atisha, and they wanted him to come and teach.
Buddhism was already established in Tibet at that point, and the story goes that it was in decline.
It's a racy story, actually.

The story goes that the tantric practitioners in Tibet of the time had gotten the idea that ethical self-discipline and tantra were mutually exclusive, and that enlightenment could be achieved through intoxication and many forms of sexual misconduct.
They were really wild at that point in Tibet.
So Atisha went up there and helped straighten them out.
One of the last things I want to say about Atisha, one of the last stories, is that he heard that the inhabitants of Tibet were really nice people, really pleasant and easy to get along with.
Instead of being delighted by that, he was concerned that he would not have enough negative emotions to work with in his practice.
It would be too nice.
The story goes that he brought along an ill-tempered Bengali servant boy who would criticize Atisha incisively, and it was really awful to spend time with, to help him practice.
Apparently Tibetan teachers to this day like to make the joke that when he arrived in Tibet he realized it was okay.
There was enough trouble and negativity, and he would be able to practice thoroughly.
The most likely story is that Atisha learned and reformulated these teachings, these mind training phrases, these slogans, from his teacher in Sumatra, who was called Dharmaraksita.
Atisha taught them and described them in his masterwork, which is called Lamp on the Path to Enlightenment, which I think still exists.
But then these teachings came to us via a twelfth century Tibetan teacher named Geshe Chekhawa, who reformulated them and wrote important commentary about them.
In some accounts he's credited with creating them, but apparently more likely he didn't create them.
More likely it came from Atisha's teacher in Sumatra.
Then they were introduced to the West by Chogyam Trungpa, who was actually reading and translating Geshe Chekhawa's book, leaping all the way back to the twelfth century into English.
I think also a little later Kelsang Gyatso did the same thing, also teaching in the West, another Tibetan teacher teaching in the West.
Kelsang Gyatso is the founder of the New Kadampa Order, which is a kind of revival of the first order that credits Atisha as their founder.
The New Kadampa Order is the group that has that center down on Bay Street, which is Dharmakirti.
They study the Lojang teachings there, and their teacher feels like he's in this lineage.
The Kadampa School actually died out, so he's a sort of reviver of that school.
I think he's a reviver of one, and there's some conflict, not to get too into this, but there's some conflict in the Tibetan world about that.
The Kadampa guys and the Sakya guys, which is Dalai Lama, are like enemies, and they have a hard time getting along.
You'd think all these peaceful Buddhist monks would get along great, but people are people.
Anyway, there's a young monk there named Norbu who studies the Lojang teachings.
So that's two important Tibetan introducers of these teachings, Trungpa Rinpoche and Kelsang Gyatso.
Then there are also two important American translators of these teachings, B.
Alan Wallace and Ken McLeod.
I've especially been appreciating Alan Wallace's comments as I've been studying them, but I haven't seen Ken McLeod's.

If you're online, you can go to lojangmindtraining.com, which is actually a very fabulous offering, a Buddhist geek project where they've got seven different translations, and you hover over here, and it all changes there, and you see what this guy said about it, and how these are organized, and it spans out in multiple dimensions, and it's great.
So, Lojang with two O's: lojangmindtraining.com.
I was reading that while I waited for the books to arrive.
I'm really happy, actually, about these teachings.
I'm really excited that Norman brought these up.
It feels very congruent with our Zen practice, because Zen does already include the contemplation of phrases.
These are phrases.
We're getting to the phrases, don't worry.
Not all of us have practiced with this very much, but practicing with phrases is an important part of our tradition.
One of the ways is working with koans.

One of the koan study methods is that you take a central phrase in the koan, and usually each koan has a traditional central phrase, and you work with just that phrase in zazen: just reciting, thinking, feeling what was there, breathing, being with that phrase, beyond thinking, just with that phrase.
What's great about that is that little by little it helps you feel a sense of continuity in practice.
Whether you're sitting or not sitting, you're always breathing, you're always bringing up your koan, your phrase.
The most famous of these phrases is the phrase from Zhao Zhou's Mu, which you've probably heard of.
A monk asked Zhao Zhou, he said, no, Mu just means no.
The Three Treasures tradition, in which Robert Aitken is a founding teacher, and locally Jack Duffy and also Peter and Terry, their teacher Nelson Foster, they're all in that tradition.
They almost always ask people to start their Zen practice by studying this koan, Mu.
We don't do that so much, but we do sometimes work, a little less formally, with koans, and we also often bring up phrases.
I practiced for a long time with the phrase "what is it?"
In every exhalation I would just ask myself, what is it?
It's not exactly even a question, just: what is it?
What is it?
Eventually it's a feeling, bringing up the spirit of questioning and inquiry.
We think we know what this is, but do we really?
What is this?
Anyway, the contemplation of phrases is part of our tradition.
But our phrases are all pointed to nowhere.
Our phrases go nowhere, which is great and also a challenge.
It's great because there is nowhere to go, and it helps us explore that more deeply.
But it's also a challenge because the mind needs something to do sometimes.
And just going nowhere, it doesn't always work out.
These Tonglen phrases are a little more directive and a little more instructive.
But we can bring to them this Zen spirit of just breathing, nowhere to go, nothing to do.

At the same time as we can appreciate some tools, some technique, some guidance, the thing we can bring to the table is our wonderful emphasis on non-attachment, non-attainment, and deeply settling into the contentment and perfection of every moment.
So we can study these and we can benefit from them, but we can bring our Zen spirit to them and not get too excited, not get too worked up about it, not feel like, okay, here's a new project.
There are 59 phrases.
I'm going to start with number one this week.
Ten years from now, I will study them all and I'll be enlightened.
It doesn't really work that way either.

In her introduction to Chogyam Trungpa's book, Training the Mind (there are many editions, I think; this is a recent edition, so I can look at this later), and Dharma teachers don't really write books, actually.
It's a seminar he did.
He's got a couple of different seminars which they edited and transcribed and organized.
So in that book, the editor talks about how to work with these phrases.
She said:
*The daily life practiced with Lojang slogans is based on spontaneous recall of appropriate slogans in the thick of daily life.

Rather than making a heavy-handed or deliberate effort to guide your actions in accordance with these slogans, a quality of spontaneous reminder is evoked through the study of these traditional aphorisms.
If you study these seven points of mind training and memorize the slogans, you will find that they arise effortlessly in your mind at the oddest of times.
They have a haunting quality, and in their reoccurrence, they can lead you gradually to a more and more subtle understanding of the nature of kindness and compassion.*
So they just pop up.
And then she says:

*And this approach to moral action, to the practice of these slogans, is one of removing obstacles of limited vision, fear, and self-clinging, so that one's actions are not burdened by the weight of self-concern, projection, and expectation.
The slogans are meant to be practiced.
That is, they need to be studied and memorized, and at the same time, they need to be let go.
They are merely conceptual tools pointing to a non-conceptual realization.*
I'll read a little bit of that again.
Working with these obstacles, we remove obstacles of limited vision, fear, self-clinging, so that our actions are not burdened by the weight of self-concern, projection, and expectation.
I thought that was a helpful phrase.
What would it be if your actions were not burdened by the weight of self-concern?

These little reminders would just pop up sometimes.
Trungpa Rinpoche was really famous for somehow popping up just what you needed at just the right time.
He had a real knack for that.
And he could even do that when he was drunk, apparently.
He's also famous for that, sadly.
I'm sure that many of his students have stories about these little signs, the right little slogan just being there when you needed it.
I don't know if Trungpa snuck around, moving them around or something.
He might well have.
Actually, I'm supposed to get together with Paul Warwick, who's a local Dharma teacher, and he was a student of Trungpa Rinpoche, so I'll try to remember to ask him.

No, I don't remember that.
So, who knows?
So, a long introduction.
Let's talk about the 59 Lojang Mind Training slogans.
We're not going to talk about all 59.
Norman did a couple of batches of them.
I'm going to do a little bit different approach.
We're going to have two talks, one now, one next week.
The 59 slogans are organized into seven points.
Rather than try to thoroughly cover a couple of the points, as Norman did, I want to just do a few slogans from each point that speak to me.
I've also made a handout that has all of them, so we'll look at the handout later.
The seven points are: number one, preliminary practice.
Number two, formal practice.
Number three, using adversity.
Number four, life and death.
Number five, yardsticks.
Number six, commitments.
And number seven, guidelines.
They're divided into seven points, each one having different numbers of slogans in them.
Tonight I want to speak about a few slogans from the first three points: preliminary practice, formal practice, and using adversity.
Then we'll try to do the other four next week with less introduction.
The first point, preliminaries, only has one slogan in it, which is, "First, train in the preliminaries."
So that's a whole lot to memorize.
This means: establish and stabilize and continue your spiritual practice.
In Zen, especially with our emphasis on beginner's mind, we can say that this is not exactly preliminary practice.
Preliminary implies you do one thing and then you're ready to do something else.
You don't need to do the first thing anymore.
But how we practice in our school is that we're always at the beginning.
At the beginning, we practice preliminary practices.
In the middle, we practice preliminary practices.
And at the end, we practice preliminary practices.

Without really touching the ground of our mind through this steady and ongoing practice, without this developed and continuous work of returning to what our deepest heart is, the way we understand it, there's really no possibility for these slogans to be transformational and help us to study the real depths of our life without this steady so-called preliminary practice over time.
Without that, the slogans are diminished.
So we would not approach this like, okay, do an intensive meditation retreat for seven days and then don't meditate anymore.
Now memorize these, now do this, now do that.
I don't really know that much in practice about how the Tibetan tradition works out.
I think they keep up meditation for their whole career, but they emphasize different things at different times.
I did read, by the way, that the Dalai Lama gets up at 3:30 in the morning every day and does four hours of practice.

And then runs the country in exile for the rest of the day.
That's a schedule for you.
So in our school, what are the preliminary practices?
Well: zazen, kinhin, walking meditation, service, chanting and bowing, working with the teacher, working with the sangha, studying the teachings.
Beyond the zendo, beyond the zendo training in these preliminary practices is our continuous awareness of breath and body and our study of the immediacy of experience.
We get out of our heads and we notice what's actually happening moment after moment.
Our preliminary, ongoing, endless preliminary practice is waking up to the life that we are actually in, over and over.
We fall asleep a little bit, we get distracted, we suffer, and suffering helps bring us back.
And we're back, maybe a little more.
But then our problem as Zen students is we might think, well, that's it.
What else would there be?
Get distracted, come back.
Okay, that's it, I've got it.
So we might think that's the whole of the practice and we might get stuck.
We might get a little dull, a little stalled.
Although we do also have techniques and teachings to help us reinvigorate and reimagine our life and our practice, these lojong teachings really seem great for that.
They're a great and helpful path for enlivening our practice and making it challenging and interesting and engaging for us to be practicing the way.
But as I was saying earlier, we need to remember that there's not really any step-wise progression here.
That's not really how it goes for human beings.
If we had the idea that we would eventually get beyond these preliminary practices, it's like saying, well, I'm really tired of being a person.
I'd like to get beyond being a person.
I'd like to be something else now.
Because our understanding of practice is that to practice these preliminary practices is just a full expression of our human life.
So that's the first point, and the first slogan in the lojong teachings, the preliminaries: "Train in the preliminaries."
The second mind training point, you're like, where's the new stuff?
It's the same old stuff.
The second mind training point could be called formal practice or the main practice.
Trungpa does a little longer title to make a point.
He says that the second training point is called the main practice, which is training in bodhicitta.
It just summarizes it in the title.
Bodhicitta, as you might know, is the mind of awakening.
The Indo-Tibetan teachings make a very big deal of bodhicitta.
It's a very central topic.
If you have studied Shantideva, or listened to Chris's wonderful talks or Norman's talks, you know that Shantideva is all about bodhicitta.
First, second chapter, all about bodhicitta.
So, what is bodhicitta?
Bodhicitta is recognizing that we have a mind that thinks thoughts, but we don't really use it very well much of the time.
We think about what I want, how to take care of myself, how to get what I need, how to avoid what I don't want.
And we may have noticed that that does not always work out the way we hoped.
So bodhicitta is suggesting we can use this mind, the same exact mind, in a much broader, more expansive, loving way.
It is actually even beyond any sort of concept of having a mind.
We can have a mind that is beyond being a mind, a mind that completely embraces love in all beings and puts others first, always.
And it's a very enthusiastic mind.
The mind of bodhicitta is the mind of just, let's do it.
There's no time to waste.
I can't be sitting around watching TV.
There are beings to save.
Bodhicitta is the mind that bodhisattvas awaken, that bodhisattvas practice.
Bodhisattvas are beings who are devoted to enlightenment, so it's a bit synonymous.
The bodhisattva is the being, and the bodhicitta is the mind of the bodhisattva.
I've been thinking a lot about this lately, and this next slogan speaks to it.
One of the essential differences between our conventional mind and the bodhicitta mind, all those slogans in this top point, is the way we divide up the world, the way we dichotomize the world.
The conventional mind is quite concerned with what is right and what is wrong, and with being right and being in the right.
So think about that for a moment.
Would you admit that you like to be right?
Is that true for you?
Do you like to be right?
It's really painful, maybe, being wrong.
Or maybe you're really a wreck and you like being wrong.
It's kind of the same thing.
So the bodhicitta mind of bodhisattvas is not at all concerned about being right.
Being right is not even on the radar.
It doesn't matter.
Being right, being wrong, not important.
Just an idea.
The bodhicitta mind of the bodhisattva is concerned with suffering and non-suffering, suffering and the end of suffering.
That's the question that is being asked, considering all actions of body and speech and mind.
And therefore the actions that arise from bodhicitta, the end of the bodhisattva, are always oriented around how can I reduce suffering?
How can I reduce suffering?
What was I trying to say here?
And the bodhicitta, in its interest in suffering, while it's a smart mind, it's an intellectual mind too, it's not just a kind of mind.
It's really considering things carefully.
The bodhicitta mind is also really studying how to determine what's suffering, what's non-suffering, what's suffering, what's not suffering in the situation.
And this teaching of that being the important inquiry is very true to the Buddha's original teachings, which is just all through the Pali Canon.
The most famous example is probably that one time the Buddha was passing through the town of a group of people called the Kalamas.
So there's a little vignette, which is now called the Kalama Sutra.
The Kalama people had recently had a lot of different spiritual teachers around.

Roving spiritual teachers were a big deal, and they were debating each other, and the Kalama people were trying to decide which teacher to pay attention to and what kind of things they should really be doing.

How do we figure out how to validate spiritual teachings?
How do we know what's right and what's wrong?
Which are the right ones?

Notice your own experience.
Study your own experience.
When you take an action, study the result.
Is it suffering or not suffering?
If it was suffering, don't do that action.
Try another action.
Really, almost scientifically, study cause and effect in your heart and your mind and in your world.
